Stage 3 · Grammar

How sure are you?

The same prediction, at five different strengths.

Read these four sentences from the radio programme.
  • This trend will definitely spread around the world.
  • That percentage is likely to rise to around 92% by 2030.
  • Other countries, like Finland, may soon follow.
  • They even think it might prevent you from becoming ill.
Which sentence is the speaker least sure about?
English grades certainty on a scale, and speakers are expected to say where they stand on it.

Probability language lets you show how confident you are that something will happen. English does not divide this into two boxes — certain and uncertain — but runs a scale from will definitely at the top, through will probably and is likely to, to may / might / could in the middle, then down through probably won’t and is unlikely to to definitely won’t at the bottom.

Marking your position on that scale is not decoration; it is a requirement of accurate speech. Forest bathing prevents illness is a claim of established fact. Forest bathing might prevent illness is a claim about a possibility — and only the second is honest if the research is still going on. In journalism, academic writing and ordinary conversation alike, overstating your certainty is treated as a failure of accuracy rather than as confidence.

The middle of the scale is occupied by three modals that are very close in meaning at this level: may, might and could. May is slightly more formal, could slightly weaker, and might is the safest default. What matters far more than choosing between them is getting their negatives right, because the pattern is not symmetrical: the negative of might is might not, never couldn’t. Couldn’t means impossible, which is a different claim altogether.

One item in this set is grammatically unlike the others and causes persistent trouble: likely is an adjective, not an adverb, despite its -ly ending. It therefore needs a form of be: It is likely to rain, never it likely rains. Its adverb equivalent is probably, which attaches to an auxiliary instead: it will probably rain.

Before you look at the table: the table below arranges the expressions from most certain to least certain and shows where the adverbs go. Position matters: probably comes after will but before won’t.
The scale, from certain to unlikely
How sureThe formExample
Certainwill definitely · won’t definitely notThis trend will definitely spread.
Very probablewill probably · is likely to · there’s a good chanceThe number is likely to rise.
Possiblemay · might · could · might wellFinland may soon follow.
Improbableprobably won’t · is unlikely toThis percentage probably won’t rise much further.
Very doubtfulI doubt (whether) · definitely won’tI doubt whether it will change anything.
Where the small words go
RuleRightWrong
probably after will, before won’tIt will probably rise. · It probably won’t rise.It probably will rise.
may / might / could + plain verbIt might rain.It might to rain.
be likely to + verbThey are likely to agree.They are likely agree.
Negative possibilityIt might not work.It mightn’t to work.

May, might and could are almost the same here. All three mean “it is possible”. May is slightly more formal; could is common when you are giving one option among several.

Careful with the negatives. It might not happen means it is possible that it will not. It won’t happen means you are certain. They are not the same strength at all.

The mistake to avoid. Be likely takes to: The number is likely to rise, never is likely rise. And after may / might / could there is never a to.

Two ways to say the same thing. There’s a good chance it will rain = It’s likely to rain = It will probably rain. Learn one of each so you do not repeat yourself.

Full grammar reference — probability — will, may, might, could, probably, be likely to

What it is

Probability language lets you say how certain you are that something will happen. English grades this on a scale rather than in two boxes: from will definitely at one end, through will probably, is likely to, may / might / could, down to probably won’t and definitely won’t at the other.

What it means, and what it does

Adding a probability marker is not decoration. Forest bathing prevents illness is a claim of fact; Forest bathing might prevent illness is a claim about a possibility, and only the second is honest if the research is unfinished. In academic, journalistic and everyday English, marking your degree of certainty is a basic requirement of accurate speech.

When and why we use it

Probability language lets you show how confident you are that something will happen. English does not divide this into two boxes — certain and uncertain — but runs a scale from will definitely at the top, through will probably and is likely to, to may / might / could in the middle, then down through probably won’t and is unlikely to to definitely won’t at the bottom.

Marking your position on that scale is not decoration; it is a requirement of accurate speech. Forest bathing prevents illness is a claim of established fact. Forest bathing might prevent illness is a claim about a possibility — and only the second is honest if the research is still going on. In journalism, academic writing and ordinary conversation alike, overstating your certainty is treated as a failure of accuracy rather than as confidence.

The middle of the scale is occupied by three modals that are very close in meaning at this level: may, might and could. May is slightly more formal, could slightly weaker, and might is the safest default. What matters far more than choosing between them is getting their negatives right, because the pattern is not symmetrical: the negative of might is might not, never couldn’t. Couldn’t means impossible, which is a different claim altogether.

One item in this set is grammatically unlike the others and causes persistent trouble: likely is an adjective, not an adverb, despite its -ly ending. It therefore needs a form of be: It is likely to rain, never it likely rains. Its adverb equivalent is probably, which attaches to an auxiliary instead: it will probably rain.

Typical situations

You need this language for talking about the future, discussing research and statistics, making forecasts, hedging a claim you cannot prove, and disagreeing with somebody who has overstated their case.

  • Near certainty — will definitely, is certain to — the speaker has no real doubt.This trend will definitely spread around the world.
  • Strong probability — will probably, is likely to, there’s a good chance.The number is likely to rise to 92% by 2030.
  • Open possibility — may, might, could — roughly a 50/50 chance; the three are close in meaning.Other countries, like Finland, may soon follow.
  • Weak possibility — might well is stronger than might; might just is weaker.It might well become as popular in Europe.
  • Improbability — probably won’t, is unlikely to, I doubt.That percentage probably won’t rise much further.
  • Impossibility in the speaker’s view — definitely won’t, there’s no chance.Governments definitely won’t fund it on that scale.

How it differs from similar structures

may / might / could = possible · must / can’t = a conclusion you are sure of. He might be at home (possible) vs He must be at home — his car’s outside (certain). Lesson 26 develops this.
likely (adjective, needs be) · probably (adverb, needs an auxiliary). It’s likely to rise = It will probably rise.

How to build it

Modal: subject + will / may / might / could + base verb
With an adverb: subject + will + definitely / probably + base verb  (but: subject + probably + won’t + base verb)
be likely to: subject + am / is / are + likely / unlikely to + base verb
It construction: It’s likely / possible that + clause
AffirmativeIt may rain. · She might agree. · They could follow.
NegativeIt may not rain. · She might not agree. — no contraction of may not.
QuestionModals of probability are not usually used in questions. Ask instead: Do you think it will rain? or Is it likely to rain?
be likely to — negativeIt isn’t likely to happen. · It is unlikely to happen.
Adverb positionafter the auxiliary: will probably rise, is definitely going to fall.
Negative adverb positionbefore the auxiliary: probably won’t rise, definitely won’t fall.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • might’ve, could’ve and may’ve are heard constantly in speech and are frequently misheard as might of. Write might have.
  • likely is stressed on the first syllable: LIKE-ly. It is an adjective, not an adverb, despite the -ly ending.
  • Certainty is often carried by stress as much as by the word: It MIGHT work (doubt) vs It might WORK (hope).

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Likely is an adjective, so it needs be: It is likely to rain, never it likely rains. This is the single most common error with this item.
  • May, might and could are practically interchangeable for future possibility at B1. May is slightly more formal; might is the safest default.
  • Couldn’t is not the negative of could here. It could rain → It might not rain. It couldn’t rain means ‘that is impossible’, which is deduction (Lesson 26).
  • May also means permission (Lesson 8). Context separates the two; in writing, might avoids the ambiguity.
  • Perhaps and maybe normally start the sentence: Maybe it will rain. They are not used after the auxiliary.
  • Do not double up markers: It will probably maybe rain. One marker per clause.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • It likely to rain tomorrow. → It’s likely to rain tomorrow.Likely is an adjective and needs be.
  • Maybe it will happen, maybe it won’t — it may possibly perhaps rise. → It may rise.Use one probability marker, not three.
  • The number will probably not rise. → The number probably won’t rise.Probably goes before a negative auxiliary.
  • It could not rain tomorrow. → It might not rain tomorrow.Couldn’t means impossible, not ‘possibly not’.
  • Forest bathing might to prevent illness. → Forest bathing might prevent illness.Modals take the base verb with no to.
  • It is likely that it will rains. → It is likely that it will rain.After will, no -s.

More examples in context

  • certainScreen use will definitely keep rising as smartphones get cheaper.
  • strong probabilityVisits to national parks are likely to fall further.
  • strong probabilityNinety-two per cent of the population will probably live in cities by 2030.
  • open possibilityWalking in a forest might even stop you getting ill.
  • open possibilityOther countries could start building their own centres.
  • stronger possibilityJapan might well build another fifty trails.
  • improbabilityPeople probably won’t give up their screens completely.
  • improbabilityA change that big is unlikely to happen quickly.
  • hedged claimIt seems possible that the trees give off something useful.
  • doubtI doubt the effect is as strong as the report suggests.

A tip for remembering it

Picture a ladder of certainty and put each expression on a rung: will definitely → is likely to / will probably → may / might / could → probably won’t / is unlikely to → definitely won’t. Before you speak, decide which rung you are on, then take the expression from that rung and nothing else.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Probability runs on a scale, from will definitely down to definitely won’t.
  2. May, might, could + base verb all express open possibility and are close in meaning.
  3. Likely is an adjective: is likely to. Probably is an adverb: will probably.
  4. Probably / definitely go after will but before won’t.
  5. The negative of might is might not, never couldn’t.
  6. Use one marker per clause — stacking them weakens the sentence.
